claims.claim: In 1665, the astronomer Cassini saw a dark oval on Jupiter.
claims.source_checked: https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2024GL108993 (doi:10.1029/2024GL108993, full text at publisher via Firecrawl scrape)
claims.note: Abstract: 'G. D. Cassini discovered in 1665 the presence of a dark oval at the GRS latitude, known as the Permanent Spot'. Sec 3.1: first reported by Cassini 'and other astronomers in July-September 1665'. The script does not claim he was first (paper mentions a possible 1632 Bandtius sighting), so no conflict.

claims.claim: Hook as heard by a viewer who swipes at second two (A4): 'In 1665, the astronomer Cassini...' / implied 'Cassini saw something on Jupiter in 1665'
claims.note: Nothing false is spoken in the first sentence: it never names the Great Red Spot, and the correction ('probably not the Great Red Spot') follows immediately. Condition: this holds only for the VO. The popular myth is 'the GRS has been seen since 1665', so the title, thumbnail, captions and opening visual must not label or show the 1665 oval as the Great Red Spot (or as red); recheck under A6 when on-screen strings exist.

claims.claim: It was probably not the Great Red Spot.
claims.note: Abstract: 'PS is unlikely to correspond to the current GRS'; Plain Language Summary: 'most likely the current GRS ... is not the Permanent Spot'; Fig. 2 caption: 'highly unlikely'. 'Probably not' matches the hedge; it does not overstate to 'was not'.

claims.claim: Astronomers kept reporting his spot until 1713.
claims.note: Sec 3.1: observed 'in 1667, 1672, 1677, 1685-1687, 1690-1691, 1694, 1708, and was last reported in 1713 by M. Maraldi'; abstract: 'observed until 1713'. Reports were intermittent, which 'kept reporting' simplifies acceptably. 'His spot' is fine as a label; the paper credits Cassini and others.

claims.claim: Then, for about a hundred and eighteen years, nobody recorded it at all.
claims.note: Sec 3.1: 'No reports of PS or any sign of its presence exists in the available observations of Jupiter between 1713 and 1831, a long period of ~118 years'; drawings by Messier 1769, Herschel 1778, Schroeter 1785-86 show no such spot. 'About' carries the '~'. 'Nobody recorded it' matches 'no reports in the available observations'.

claims.claim: The storm we call the Great Red Spot first shows up in drawings in 1831.
claims.note: Sec 3.1: 'The first drawings showing the signature of the current GRS, recorded by its Hollow, date back to 1831'; abstract: 'first observed in 1831'. What shows in 1831 is the Hollow, not a red oval (reddish only ~1872-1876), so visuals at 1831 must not show a red spot.

claims.claim: And Cassini's spot was only a third to a half as long as the Great Red Spot was in 1879.
claims.note: Sec 3.2: 'The length of PS is 2-3 times smaller than that of the 1879 GRS.' 2-3 times smaller = 1/2 to 1/3 of the length. 'Long' = east-west (zonal) length, as in the paper. The comparison is with the 1879 red oval, not the larger 1831-1877 Hollow (~50-60 deg), so it must not be visualised against the Hollow.

claims.claim: To be the same storm, it would have had to keep growing for more than a century, unseen.
claims.note: Sec 3.2: 'PS would have had to grow steadily from 1713 to 1879 at a rate of ~+0.14 deg/year (160 km/year) to be the GRS. This is highly unlikely since ... no reports of PS or GRS exist during this long period'. 1713-1879 = 166 years; even the fully unrecorded stretch 1713-1831 is 118 years, so 'more than a century, unseen' holds on either reading.

claims.claim: No storm on Jupiter has ever been seen to grow like that.
claims.note: Sec 3.2: 'no continuously sustained grow in size has been never reported in Jupiter's vortices' (citing Ingersoll et al. 2004; Rogers 1995). 'Like that' must mean sustained, century-long growth: the paper itself reports a transient GRS length increase 1927-1939 and vortex mergers producing larger ovals, so the line would be false without 'like that'. Keep the qualifier.

claims.claim: So the Great Red Spot has been on record for nearly two hundred years.
claims.note: Sec 3.1: 'The current GRS has therefore certainly been in existence for 193 years' (paper published 2024, counting from 1831). 1831 to 2026 = 195 years, so 'nearly two hundred' is correct now. 'On record' correctly frames 1831 as first record, not formation date (Sec 4.3 suggests a proto-GRS cell earlier, possibly ~70 deg long by 1725 by extrapolation).

claims.claim: Cassini's spot was most likely a different storm, long gone.
claims.note: Sec 3.1: 'it is most likely that this lack of observations during such a large period means that PS disappeared'; Plain Language Summary: 'most likely the current GRS ... is not the Permanent Spot'. 'Most likely' keeps the paper's hedge; 'long gone' = disappeared after 1713.
